title: Trans-scale crystal dynamics for controlling kinetic responses in organic molecular systems

paper_content.abstract: The origin and control of material dynamics are fundamental to understanding functional systems from molecular assemblies to engineered devices. The ability to actively control and directly visualize rapid chemical and structural changes in a single crystal remains a major challenge in solid-state chemistry, limiting our understanding of dynamic functions in molecular materials. Here, we report an anthracene-based molecular crystal platform that enables dual physical control of solid-state [4+4] photocycloaddition through temperature and light. Chemically engineered 1,8-bis(pentafluorophenyl)anthracene single crystals construct photoactive face-to-face π-stacks, allowing the reaction to be induced by visible-light irradiation. The crystals exhibit thermally switchable on/off reaction states controlled by the accumulation of lattice strain accelerated by heating. Furthermore, we observe the reaction and dynamics under various light sources, including UV, white LED, laser, and sunlight, demonstrating dual controllability by heat and light. Importantly, weak light irradiation with an LED enables direct observation of intermediate states in the single crystal, revealing a correlation between lattice strain and photoconversion rate. On these bases, we identify that the reaction kinetics depend on the light propagation direction and the relative orientation of the molecular transition dipole moment, providing a new parameter for directional photodynamic control. This trans-scale approach, integrating chemical molecular packing design, photo-thermal science, and anisotropic parameters, establishes a general strategy for tunable and observable crystal dynamics.

paper_content.results:
Chemical approaches for crystal dynamics
The importance of controlling crystal dynamics through photoactivation lies in the ability to construct reactive molecular assemblies that offer high reproducibility, along with a phase transition system that enables direct observation of dynamic processes. The [4+4] photocycloaddition of anthracene represents an ideal molecular system, wherein ON–OFF structural changes can be chemically and strategically induced by modifying the substituents. To achieve a photoinduced single-crystal-to-single-crystal phase transition in anthracene derivatives, precise control over bimolecular aggregation and crystal packing is essential. We targeted a face-to-face anthracene arrangement—favorable for photodimerization—by introducing substituents at the 1,8-positions along the short axis. The minimum face-to-face π-stacked structure required for the ON reaction has been identified based on data from the crystal structure database, previous literature, and our own study using molecular electrostatic potential maps. Electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups were selected to tune intermolecular interactions, thereby steering the packing toward either face-to-face or edge-to-face conformations. 1,8-Bis(perfluorophenyl)anthracene (1) was prepared by direct arylation (75% yield), while 1,8-bis(4-fluorophenyl)anthracene (2), 1,8-bisphenylanthracene (3), 1,8-bis(4-methylphenyl)anthracene (4), and 1,8-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)anthracene (5) were synthesized by Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling (58–98% yields). Vapor diffusion or solvent evaporation afforded single crystals (1_CCDC:2456683, 2_CCDC:2456863, 3a_CCDC:2456867, 3b_CCDC:2456866, 4_CCDC:2456864, and 5_CCDC:2456865). Depending on the choice of electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups, 1,8-diarylanthracene adopts either an ON (face-to-face) or OFF (edge-to-face) stacking structure in crystal.

1,8-Bis(pentafluorophenyl)anthracene (1) (Fig. 2a), which promotes selective face-to-face stacking through the introduction of electron-withdrawing groups and exhibits a characteristic optical absorption band, demonstrates ON behavior in crystal dynamics upon visible light irradiation. At 303 K, the centroid–centroid distances between the anthracene units in Unit 1 and Unit 2 are 3.818 and 4.667 Å, with corresponding overlap ratios of 41% and 33%, respectively. Notably, the centroid–centroid distance in Unit 1 is less than 4.2 Å, satisfying Schmidt’s criterion for [4+4] photocycloaddition. These results demonstrate that photodimerization occurs selectively at the Unit 1 site within a single crystal upon light irradiation. The resulting photodimer (1_PD) forms specifically at this position. Although the 1_PD crystals retain the original space group P2₁/c, Raman spectroscopy reveals changes in intra- and intermolecular vibrational modes, indicating modifications to both the chemical structure and crystal lattice. A Raman-active intramolecular vibrational mode at 329 cm⁻¹ was observed, arising from the C–C single bond formed through photodimerization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reverse transformation from crystalline 1_PD to crystalline 1 is feasible. This reversal was achieved by flash vacuum pyrolysis, in which specific molecular bonds are cleaved by a momentary high-temperature treatment. The results of this reverse reaction were also confirmed by NMR and single crystal structure analysis. These findings indicate that crystal dynamics can be reversibly controlled by the combined use of light and heat. These findings provide direct evidence for previously unobserved trans-scale crystal dynamics, governed by light-induced structural switching and kinetic control.

Thermal control of crystal dynamics
As crystal dynamics arise from the release of lattice strain accumulated during dimerization, thermal expansion or contraction of the unit cell induces the buildup of such strain. To investigate this, we performed variable-temperature single-crystal X-ray diffraction of crystal 1 from 103 to 303 K, evaluating atomic displacement parameters (U_eq) and crystallographic thermal expansion. With increasing temperature, two key changes were observed: (1) U_eq values of C9 and C10—atoms directly involved in anthracene photodimerization—increased, and (2) the reaction gap widened due to increased intermolecular distances (d_centroid-centroid, d_π-π, d_parallel) between Units 1 and 2. Expansion of the gap between π-stacks also induced anisotropic thermal expansion along the crystallographic c-axis and a reduction in the β angle. The temperature dependence of the photoreaction under white LED irradiation reveals that the crystal undergoes anisotropic deformation of the unit lattice as the temperature increases. It shows an “OFF: dormant state” between 103 and 203 K, during which no reaction occurs over 360 s, while a “ON: photoactive state” is observed between 253 and 353 K. Interestingly, the response time decreases with increasing temperature. Notably, under these conditions, crystal dynamics can be controlled in an ON–OFF manner by using temperature as a secondary physical parameter.

Optical control of crystal dynamics
The response time can also be modulated by photophysical parameters such as light intensity and wavelength. In contrast to white LED irradiation at room temperature (298 ± 5 K), UV light irradiation caused severe crystal collapse, including jumping, fragmentation, explosion, splintering, cracking, and splitting. Simultaneously, the emission color shifted from green to blue with increasing light exposure time. Single crystal X-ray structural analysis confirmed that the crystal obtained by UV irradiation (CCDC: 2483421) was structurally and chemically identical to the final product obtained by white LED irradiation, 1_PD. Similar behavior was observed under blue laser or sunlight exposure, though the response speed varied depending on the light source. Historically, the [4+4] photocycloaddition in crystals was proposed to require reactive sites to be within 4.2 Å of each other, and this was verified using UV light. Whereas crystal dynamics were previously accessible essentially under UV light, the discovery of systems responsive to visible light has enabled a more hierarchical and detailed understanding of photoinduced single-crystal-to-single-crystal phase transition-based dynamic processes. This UV-visible-driven dynamic crystal may exhibit varying phase transition ratios depending on the light wavelength. Powder X-ray diffraction measurements under UV irradiation at room temperature revealed that the diffraction intensity of the {020} reflection of crystalline 1 gradually disappeared with increasing irradiation time. This observation indicates a structural transition from crystalline 1 to crystalline 1_PD under UV irradiation. The {020} reflection from crystal 1 completely disappeared within approximately 210 s, demonstrating the quantitative transformation to crystal 1_PD. Under white LED irradiation, however, the phase transition (conversion) rate reached only about 50% within a comparable irradiation time. This difference arises from the higher absorption coefficient of UV light relative to visible light, confirming that the phase transition rate depends on the wavelength of the incident light. The absorption edge of one crystal, calculated from the fluorescence excitation spectrum, was found to be 470 nm, indicating a clear response to visible light.

Observation of intermediate states
While the mechanism of crystal dynamics was previously inferred by comparing crystal structures before and after the reaction, the stepwise photoreaction of the crystal, induced by white LED irradiation (a weak excitation light source) at room temperature, allows for direct observation of intermediate states, providing insights into the mechanism. The state corresponds to a mixed crystal 1·1_PD (x, y) with a nonstoichiometric composition, where crystals 1 and 1_PD coexist. The lattice parameter decreased linearly with increasing conversion ratio y. As unit 1 is progressively replaced by 1_PD, Vegard’s law predicts values of y as 0.87 and 0.92 at 480 and 540 s, respectively, based on the lattice constant a. The kinetics evaluated by the Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov (JMAK) equation were determined to be k = 3.5 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ and n = 1.3. Since n > 1, it was shown that 1_PD formed in the crystal acts as an autocatalyst for unreacted Unit 1. Photoinduced crystal dynamics based on the process of releasing the lattice strain stored by the photoproduct to the outside reveal the correlation between the conversion ratio of the intermediate state and the lattice strain (Δa/a_0, Δb/b_0, Δc/c_0) and the change in the lattice constants (Δa, Δb, Δc), leading to their control. While Δb/b_0 and Δc/c_0 change very little with increasing y, Δa/a_0 decreases significantly with increasing y, indicating that lattice strain accumulates in the crystallographic a-axis direction as the photoreaction progresses. At this constant temperature, photoinduced lattice deformation reduces the β angle like the heating process. The identification of this correlation between the conversion ratio and lattice strain supports the mechanism by which thermally controlled ON/OFF crystal dynamics and response speed are driven by the promotion of lattice strain storage as the temperature increases.

Directional photodynamic control in crystal
The origin of this dynamic process suggests that the orientational light absorption efficiency of the higher-order structure controls the reaction probability. The crystal structure reveals that the transition dipole moment (μ), which correlates with the absorption coefficient (allowed transition), is oriented along the short axis of anthracene for both Unit 1 and Unit 2. Thus, μ is oriented along the crystallographic b-axis. Because the interaction between μ and the incident electric field depends on their relative orientation, the optical absorption of the crystal is inherently anisotropic. This orientation of μ induces anisotropic optical absorption, as the efficiency of the interaction between the electric field and μ varies with the relative alignment (parallel or perpendicular) between the polarization of the incident light and μ. Light irradiation along the [010] direction results in isotropic light absorption, as the polarized light propagating in this direction is perpendicular to μ. In contrast, light irradiation along the [001] direction leads to anisotropic light absorption, as the polarized light in this direction is parallel to μ. To further explore the anisotropic nature of the reaction, we investigated the effect of light polarization on the [001] and [010] crystal planes using a white LED. Along the [010] direction, no color was observed regardless of the polarization angle, indicating isotropic light absorption for this orientation. In contrast, the [001] direction exhibited coloration at polarization angles of 0° and 180°, whereas no color appeared between 50° and 130°. These results qualitatively demonstrate anisotropic light absorption along the [001] direction, and the observed polarization dependence is consistent with the theoretically predicted orientation of μ. The photoreactive frequency factor and response time exhibit different dynamic behaviors depending on the crystal plane direction of light irradiation, due to the anisotropic molecular orientation and alignment of the molecular crystals. The frequency and response time of white LED irradiation on each plane of a single crystal were 39% of the total in the [001] direction, while they were 90% of the total in the [010] direction. These results statistically show that the [010] direction has a higher probability of occurrence than the [001] direction. The response times for the [001] direction ranged from 30 to 176 s, with a mean of 94 ± 35 s (mean ± SD, n = 90). In contrast, the response times for the [010] direction ranged from 5 to 121 s, with a mean of 34 ± 18 s (mean ± SD, n = 39). The response time is statistically shorter in the [010] direction than in the [001] direction. Since the strength of μ correlates with the efficiency of light absorption, both its direction and strength are important parameters for controlling the photoreaction rate in the solid phase. Designing both the direction and strength of μ offers the potential for even greater precision.

In summary, we have demonstrated that a trans-scale strategy, which combines appropriate physical parameters (temperature, light intensity, wavelength, and direction) with a chemical approach and a multiscale understanding of behavior from the nano- to meso- to macro-scale, can enable the control of crystal dynamics. This strategy may be applied to understanding the origin of photoreaction processes in living organisms and to controlling systems made of solid materials. Controlling physical functions based on the atomic–molecular coordinate information of a crystal structure represents a significant challenge in developing material-motion-responsive systems. We have already succeeded in providing the necessary physical parameters, which could lead to the discovery of operational dynamic devices spanning nano- to meso- to macro-scale response systems.
paper_content.methods:
Materials
Solvents and reagents were purchased from Tokyo Chemical Industry Co., Sigma-Aldrich Co., LLC, Kanto Chemical Co., Inc., and FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical. 1 was prepared by direct arylation. Purified water was obtained using an ion exchange method (Pureline WL200, Yamato Scientific). The ion exchanger resin cartridge (CPC-P) had a capacity of 2 L and contained activated carbon. The water sample had a conductivity of 0.04 × 10⁻⁴ S/m.

Equipment
¹H and ¹³C NMR spectra were recorded on a JEOL JNM-ECZ400S spectrometer and Bruker Ascend-400 spectrometers. Ultraviolet-visible (UV–vis) absorption spectroscopy was performed using a JASCO V-650 spectrophotometer. Fluorescence excitation and photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy were conducted using a JASCO FP-8300 fluorescence spectrophotometer. Optical microscopy images and movies were acquired using a SHIMADZU Moticam 1080BMH equipped with a UV lamp (365 nm, 66 mW), a microscopic photoluminescence (µ-PL) spectroscopy system with a blue laser (405 nm, 5 µW), and a KEYENCE VHX-S8000 equipped with a white LED (4 mW). Light source spectra were measured using a Color Compass MFA. The power of the light sources was measured using a Field Mate laser power meter with a PM10 power sensor. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction measurements were performed using a Rigaku XtaLAB Synergy-S/Mo system (MoKα radiation, λ = 0.71073 Å) equipped with a HyPix-600HE photon counting detector and processed using the Olex2 software package. Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were carried out using a Rigaku SmartLab diffractometer with graphite-monochromatized CuKα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å). Raman spectroscopy was conducted using a HORIBA Jobin-Yvon LabRAM HR800 spectrometer, employing an Nd:YAG laser (λ = 532 nm) as the excitation source. An area of approximately 30 µm on the sample was irradiated through a D2 filter using a 50× objective lens. A microscope-compatible cooling/heating stage (Linkam model 10002L) was used under a nitrogen atmosphere over the temperature range of 103 K–353 K.

Single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis
The reduction and correction of the diffraction data were performed using the CrysAlisPro program. The structure was solved with the ShelXT structures solution program using Intrinsic Phasing. The structure was refined with the ShelXL refinement package using Least Squares minimization. Any alerts in the CIF should be carefully addressed with the guidance of a crystallographer when necessary. The occupancies of the molecules were refined based on electron densities using the free variables. The crystallographic refinement process includes the handling of disordered molecules. All non-hydrogen atoms were refined with anisotropic displacement parameters. Hydrogen atoms were placed in idealized positions and refined as rigid atoms with the relative isotropic displacement parameters.

Theoretical calculations
All density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using Becke’s three-parameter hybrid exchange function and the Lee-Yang-Paar correlation function (B3LYP) with a default threshold of 6–31+G(d,p) basis set as implemented in Gaussian 16 Revision B.01. TD-DFT vertical excitation energy calculations were carried out for the anthracene dimers extracted from crystal structures using long-range corrected hybrid functional with damped dispersion correction (ωB97X-D). The electrostatic potential maps, highest-energy occupied, and lowest-energy unoccupied molecular orbitals were plotted using GaussView 6.0. The orientation of the transition μ was evaluated by TD-DFT calculations. Using dummy atoms to define the x, y, and z axes, the dipole vector was found to lie along the short axis of the anthracene framework.

JMAK equation
Photochemical reaction in a single crystal was modeled using the JMAK equation.

y = 1 − e⁻(kt)n (1)

where y is the conversion ratio for the 1_PD, k is the reaction ratio constant, t is the irradiation time, and n is the Avrami exponent (reaction order).

Data availability
All data that support the findings of this study are presented in the Manuscript and Supplementary Information or are available from the corresponding author upon request. The X-ray crystallographic coordinates for structures reported in this study have been deposited at the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Center (CCDC), under deposition numbers 2456683, 2456863, 2456867, 2456866, 2456864, and 2456865. These data can be obtained free of charge from The Cambridge Crystallographic Data Center via www.ccdc.cam.ac.uk/data_request/cif. Crystal dynamic movies are available as follows; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15694836.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript presents a compelling interdisciplinary study on trans-scale crystal dynamics in anthracene derivatives, demonstrating innovative control of solid-state kinetics through chemical design and physical parameters (light direction, temperature). The work provides valuable mechanistic insights into photoinduced lattice strain and anisotropic responses. While scientifically sound and suitable for publication, minor revisions are required to enhance clarity, rigor, and presentation consistency.
1. In the manuscript, the crystal dynamics in photoreaction processes of crystal 1 was comprehensively studied. However, crystal 2-5 as control samples were rarely mentioned. The authors should add some discussion to explain the meanings of each crystal reported in the article.
2. The severe crystal collapse observed under UV light compared to visible light/LED is attributed to the light wavelength. However, UV light sources often have significantly higher photon energies and potentially higher intensities (power densities) than the visible light sources used (white LED, blue laser, sunlight). The manuscript does not report the incident light intensities/power densities for the different sources used in these comparative experiments. The authors should reconsider this issue.
3. In the temperature dependence of the photoreaction, the authors claimed that：“each temperature point represents the average response time of up to three crystals“. Such sample size is not enough for statistical experiment, which is recommended to be increased to 10 or more.
4. Spelling mistake: “Date ware” (Fig.4 caption) → “Data were”
5. please confirm the format of the references.
6. Some literature (Research 2024, 7, 0411; Adv. Sci. 2025, 12, e09088) should be added to reflect the research breadth of the work.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript presents an interesting study on anthracene-based crystals that show stimuli-responsive behavior through light-induced dimerization. Although this is a well-known photochemical reaction and have been previously used as a solid platform for exploring dynamic structural changes in the solid state, in this manuscript the authors introduce a dual control mechanism—using both heat and light—to modulate the crystal’s response, allowing the visualization of intermediate states, which is a notable achievement.
However, despite these strengths, the manuscript has several issues that make it unsuitable for publication in a high-impact journal in its current form:
Comments
1) The abstract lacks specificity and fails to clearly state the focus on anthracene derivatives or highlight the key findings—namely, dual control and intermediate state visualization. Instead, it relies on vague references to biological systems, which are not directly relevant and overgeneralize the study’s implications. It should be rewritten accordingly.
2) The rationale behind the selection and design of the anthracene derivatives is not explained. Although several anthracene derivatives are synthesized and characterized, in the manuscript their specific roles are unclear. A schematic framework is needed to clarify how these derivatives contribute to the study’s objectives.
3) As the author notes, identifying the relative orientation between light propagation and the molecular transition dipole moment as a control parameter in the photodynamic process is potentially significant. However, this concept is underdeveloped in the manuscript. To substantiate its importance, the authors should provide more robust theoretical/experimental evidence than simple statistics.
4) Several figures in the Supporting Information are either incorrectly referenced or not well integrated into the main text. This weakens the clarity and coherence of the experimental narrative. Proper cross-referencing and clearer integration are needed to improve consistency and readability throughout the manuscript. For example, in page 3 the authors mention: “Raman spectroscopy reveals changes in intra- and intermolecular vibrational modes (Supplementary Fig. 18), indicating modifications to both the chemical structure and crystal lattice (Supplementary Figs. 19–21 and Supplementary Table 8)”. On the one hand, Supplementary Fig. 18 presents only two Raman spectra without any accompanying discussion of the observed differences, which limits its usefulness in supporting the claims made in the main text. On the other hand, Supplementary Figs. 19–20 primarily focus on the solid-state retro reaction, including thermal analysis (DSC and TGA), the experimental setup, and NMR characterization of the final product—none of which directly support the discussion on changes in chemical structure or crystal lattice. This misalignment highlights the need for more accurate and purposeful cross-referencing of the supplementary materials. Considering the substantial volume of Supporting Information provided, and to improve overall readability and coherence, the manuscript should be carefully revised to ensure that each supplementary figure and table is clearly and correctly cited in context, and that the integration of this material meaningfully supports the corresponding sections of the main text.
5) The authors study the transformation under different light sources; however, these reactions appear to proceed more rapidly and, in some cases, lead to the rapid breakdown of the crystals. It remains unclear whether the final phases obtained under these alternative light sources are the same as those formed under white LED light. The authors should clarify whether the photoproducts are structurally and chemically identical across different irradiation conditions, and, if not, provide a discussion on the observed differences and their implications.
In summary: While the results are of scientific interest a more focused presentation and clearer methodological framing are needed to meet the standards of a high-impact journal.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In the manuscript titled “Trans-scale crystal dynamics for controlling kinetic responses in organic molecular systems”, Hino et al. report temperature-dependent, photoinduced crystal dynamics in anthracene derivative crystals.
A key highlight of the study is the controlled modulation of crystal behavior through the relative orientation between the light propagation direction and the molecular transition dipole moment.
The work is intriguing and of have relevance to the field of dynamic molecular crystals. However, I recommend major revision before the manuscript can be considered for publication. The following points should be addressed to improve clarity, completeness, and presentation:
1. The abstract is too general and lacks a concise summary of the actual experimental work carried out. Instead of briefly stating the methodology or system studied, the abstract reads more like a conclusion. This diminishes clarity for readers attempting to understand the work from the outset.
2. The manuscript lacks a systematic description. For instance, it is not clearly stated how many anthracene derivatives were synthesized and studied, or the rationale behind their selection. The use of abbreviations should also be defined clearly at the beginning. From Figure 1 and the Supplementary Information (SI), it appears that five derivatives were investigated, but this should be clearly presented in the main text.
3. There is excessive referencing to the SI, which makes reading cumbersome. For example:
The sentence: “Depending on the choice of substituents, 1,8-diarylanthracene adopts either an ON (face-to-face) or OFF (edge-to-face) stacking structure (Supplementary Tables 1–6)” directs the reader across six different supplementary tables. A consolidated explanation in the main text summarizing this trend would help.
Similarly, the statement: “The minimum face-to-face π-stacked structure required for the ON reaction has been identified based on data from the crystal structure database, previous literature, and our own study using molecular electrostatic potential maps (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Figs. 1–13)” references 13 supplementary figures. Such heavy dependence on SI should be minimized by integrating key insights and summaries into the main text.
4. The sentence: “The discovery of crystal dynamics driven by visible light overcomes previous limitations related to light wavelength, enabling a more hierarchical and in-depth understanding of the dynamic process.” is unclear and should be elaborated. What limitations were previously imposed by light wavelength, and how does visible light resolve them?
5. The manuscript would benefit from a more detailed explanation of what exactly constitutes the ON and OFF states in terms of molecular stacking and crystal structure. These structural transitions are central to the work but are only briefly mentioned.
6. It is stated that UV light irradiation caused dramatic physical responses such as jumping, fragmentation, explosion, splintering, cracking, and splitting. But no detailed mechanism or conditions under which these movements occur is provided. Moreover, the photographic evidence (e.g., in the SI) is insufficient to clearly distinguish these effects.
7. The statement that “the crystal may exhibit varying phase transition ratios depending on the light wavelength” is not substantiated with any mechanistic explanation or data discussion. The authors should clarify the origin of this behavior.
8. Crucial details such as the intensity (power density) of the light sources used (UV, white LED, laser) are not provided. These are essential for reproducibility and understanding the kinetics.
9. Among three crystals irradiated, only one shows cracking. The authors should discuss why the other two did not respond similarly. Could crystal size or morphology be influencing the mechanical response? A brief analysis or hypothesis on size-dependence would add value.
10. The manuscript states that the transition dipole moment is oriented along the crystallographic b-axis. However, a more detailed explanation is needed on how μ is calculated or estimated from the crystal structure.
11. The manuscript focuses on the direction of the transition dipole moment but does not discuss how its magnitude might influence the photoinduced response. A brief discussion of whether higher μ would correlate with stronger or faster response would be useful, especially in the context of designing molecules for better dynamic behavior.

## Abstract

The origin and control of material dynamics are fundamental to understanding functional systems from molecular assemblies to engineered devices. The ability to actively control and directly visualize rapid chemical and structural changes in a single crystal remains a major challenge in solid-state chemistry, limiting our understanding of dynamic functions in molecular materials. Here, we report an anthracene-based molecular crystal platform that enables dual physical control of solid-state [4+4] photocycloaddition through temperature and light. Chemically engineered 1,8-bis(pentafluorophenyl)anthracene single crystals construct photoactive face-to-face π-stacks, allowing the reaction to be induced by visible-light irradiation. The crystals exhibit thermally switchable on/off reaction states controlled by the accumulation of lattice strain accelerated by heating. Furthermore, we observe the reaction and dynamics under various light sources, including UV, white LED, laser, and sunlight, demonstrating dual controllability by heat and light. Importantly, weak light irradiation with an LED enables direct observation of intermediate states in the single crystal, revealing a correlation between lattice strain and photoconversion rate. On these bases, we identify that the reaction kinetics depend on the light propagation direction and the relative orientation of the molecular transition dipole moment, providing a new parameter for directional photodynamic control. This trans-scale approach, integrating chemical molecular packing design, photo-thermal science, and anisotropic parameters, establishes a general strategy for tunable and observable crystal dynamics.

## Results

Chemical approaches for crystal dynamics
The importance of controlling crystal dynamics through photoactivation lies in the ability to construct reactive molecular assemblies that offer high reproducibility, along with a phase transition system that enables direct observation of dynamic processes. The [4+4] photocycloaddition of anthracene represents an ideal molecular system, wherein ON–OFF structural changes can be chemically and strategically induced by modifying the substituents. To achieve a photoinduced single-crystal-to-single-crystal phase transition in anthracene derivatives, precise control over bimolecular aggregation and crystal packing is essential. We targeted a face-to-face anthracene arrangement—favorable for photodimerization—by introducing substituents at the 1,8-positions along the short axis. The minimum face-to-face π-stacked structure required for the ON reaction has been identified based on data from the crystal structure database, previous literature, and our own study using molecular electrostatic potential maps. Electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups were selected to tune intermolecular interactions, thereby steering the packing toward either face-to-face or edge-to-face conformations. 1,8-Bis(perfluorophenyl)anthracene (1) was prepared by direct arylation (75% yield), while 1,8-bis(4-fluorophenyl)anthracene (2), 1,8-bisphenylanthracene (3), 1,8-bis(4-methylphenyl)anthracene (4), and 1,8-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)anthracene (5) were synthesized by Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling (58–98% yields). Vapor diffusion or solvent evaporation afforded single crystals (1_CCDC:2456683, 2_CCDC:2456863, 3a_CCDC:2456867, 3b_CCDC:2456866, 4_CCDC:2456864, and 5_CCDC:2456865). Depending on the choice of electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups, 1,8-diarylanthracene adopts either an ON (face-to-face) or OFF (edge-to-face) stacking structure in crystal.

1,8-Bis(pentafluorophenyl)anthracene (1) (Fig. 2a), which promotes selective face-to-face stacking through the introduction of electron-withdrawing groups and exhibits a characteristic optical absorption band, demonstrates ON behavior in crystal dynamics upon visible light irradiation. At 303 K, the centroid–centroid distances between the anthracene units in Unit 1 and Unit 2 are 3.818 and 4.667 Å, with corresponding overlap ratios of 41% and 33%, respectively. Notably, the centroid–centroid distance in Unit 1 is less than 4.2 Å, satisfying Schmidt’s criterion for [4+4] photocycloaddition. These results demonstrate that photodimerization occurs selectively at the Unit 1 site within a single crystal upon light irradiation. The resulting photodimer (1_PD) forms specifically at this position. Although the 1_PD crystals retain the original space group P2₁/c, Raman spectroscopy reveals changes in intra- and intermolecular vibrational modes, indicating modifications to both the chemical structure and crystal lattice. A Raman-active intramolecular vibrational mode at 329 cm⁻¹ was observed, arising from the C–C single bond formed through photodimerization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reverse transformation from crystalline 1_PD to crystalline 1 is feasible. This reversal was achieved by flash vacuum pyrolysis, in which specific molecular bonds are cleaved by a momentary high-temperature treatment. The results of this reverse reaction were also confirmed by NMR and single crystal structure analysis. These findings indicate that crystal dynamics can be reversibly controlled by the combined use of light and heat. These findings provide direct evidence for previously unobserved trans-scale crystal dynamics, governed by light-induced structural switching and kinetic control.

Thermal control of crystal dynamics
As crystal dynamics arise from the release of lattice strain accumulated during dimerization, thermal expansion or contraction of the unit cell induces the buildup of such strain. The response time can also be modulated by photophysical parameters such as light intensity and wavelength. The kinetics evaluated by the Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov (JMAK) equation were determined to be k = 3.5 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ and n = 1.3. The origin of this dynamic process suggests that the orientational light absorption efficiency of the higher-order structure controls the reaction probability. The crystal structure reveals that the transition dipole moment (μ), which correlates with the absorption coefficient (allowed transition), is oriented along the short axis of anthracene for both Unit 1 and Unit 2. Thus, μ is oriented along the crystallographic b-axis. Because the interaction between μ and the incident electric field depends on their relative orientation, the optical absorption of the crystal is inherently anisotropic. This orientation of μ induces anisotropic optical absorption, as the efficiency of the interaction between the electric field and μ varies with the relative alignment (parallel or perpendicular) between the polarization of the incident light and μ. Thus, μ is oriented along the crystallographic b-axis. Because the interaction between μ and the incident electric field depends on their relative orientation, the optical absorption of the crystal is inherently anisotropic. This orientation of μ induces anisotropic optical absorption, as the efficiency of the interaction between the electric field and μ varies with the relative alignment (parallel or perpendicular) between the polarization of the incident light and μ. Light irradiation along the [010] direction results in isotropic light absorption, as the polarized light propagating in this direction is perpendicular to μ. In contrast, light irradiation along the [001] direction leads to anisotropic light absorption, as the polarized light in this direction is parallel to μ. To further explore the anisotropic nature of the reaction, we investigated the effect of light polarization on the [001] and [010] crystal planes using a white LED. Along the [010] direction, no color was observed regardless of the polarization angle, indicating isotropic light absorption for this orientation. In contrast, the [001] direction exhibited coloration at polarization angles of 0° and 180°, whereas no color appeared between 50° and 130°. These results qualitatively demonstrate anisotropic light absorption along the [001] direction, and the observed polarization dependence is consistent with the theoretically predicted orientation of μ. The photoreactive frequency factor and response time exhibit different dynamic behaviors depending on the crystal plane direction of light irradiation, due to the anisotropic molecular orientation and alignment of the molecular crystals. The frequency and response time of white LED irradiation on each plane of a single crystal were 39% of the total in the [001] direction, while they were 90% of the total in the [010] direction. These results statistically show that the [010] direction has a higher probability of occurrence than the [001] direction. The response times for the [001] direction ranged from 30 to 176 s, with a mean of 94 ± 35 s (mean ± SD, n = 90). In contrast, the response times for the [010] direction ranged from 5 to 121 s, with a mean of 34 ± 18 s (mean ± SD, n = 39). The response time is statistically shorter in the [010] direction than in the [001] direction. Since the strength of μ correlates with the efficiency of light absorption, both its direction and strength are important parameters for controlling the photoreaction rate in the solid phase. Designing both the direction and strength of μ offers the potential for even greater precision.

In summary, we have demonstrated that a trans-scale strategy, which combines appropriate physical parameters (temperature, light intensity, wavelength, and direction) with a chemical approach and a multiscale understanding of behavior from the nano- to meso- to macro-scale, can enable the control of crystal dynamics. This strategy may be applied to understanding the origin of photoreaction processes in living organisms and to controlling systems made of solid materials. Controlling physical functions based on the atomic–molecular coordinate information of a crystal structure represents a significant challenge in developing material-motion-responsive systems. We have already succeeded in providing the necessary physical parameters, which could lead to the discovery of operational dynamic devices spanning nano- to meso- to macro-scale response systems.

## Methods

Materials
Solvents and reagents were purchased from Tokyo Chemical Industry Co., Sigma-Aldrich Co., LLC, Kanto Chemical Co., Inc., and FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical. 1 was prepared by direct arylation. Purified water was obtained using an ion exchange method (Pureline WL200, Yamato Scientific). The ion exchanger resin cartridge (CPC-P) had a capacity of 2 L and contained activated carbon. The water sample had a conductivity of 0.04 × 10⁻⁴ S/m.

Equipment
¹H and ¹³C NMR spectra were recorded on a JEOL JNM-ECZ400S spectrometer and Bruker Ascend-400 spectrometers. Ultraviolet-visible (UV–vis) absorption spectroscopy was performed using a JASCO V-650 spectrophotometer. Fluorescence excitation and photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy were conducted using a JASCO FP-8300 fluorescence spectrophotometer. Optical microscopy images and movies were acquired using a SHIMADZU Moticam 1080BMH equipped with a UV lamp (365 nm, 66 mW), a microscopic photoluminescence (µ-PL) spectroscopy system with a blue laser (405 nm, 5 µW), and a KEYENCE VHX-S8000 equipped with a white LED (4 mW). Light source spectra were measured using a Color Compass MFA. The power of the light sources was measured using a Field Mate laser power meter with a PM10 power sensor. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction measurements were performed using a Rigaku XtaLAB Synergy-S/Mo system (MoKα radiation, λ = 0.71073 Å) equipped with a HyPix-600HE photon counting detector and processed using the Olex2 software package. Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were carried out using a Rigaku SmartLab diffractometer with graphite-monochromatized CuKα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å). Raman spectroscopy was conducted using a HORIBA Jobin-Yvon LabRAM HR800 spectrometer, employing an Nd:YAG laser (λ = 532 nm) as the excitation source. An area of approximately 30 µm on the sample was irradiated through a D2 filter using a 50× objective lens. A microscope-compatible cooling/heating stage (Linkam model 10002L) was used under a nitrogen atmosphere over the temperature range of 103 K–353 K.

Single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis
The reduction and correction of the diffraction data were performed using the CrysAlisPro program. The structure was solved with the ShelXT structures solution program using Intrinsic Phasing. The structure was refined with the ShelXL refinement package using Least Squares minimization. Any alerts in the CIF should be carefully addressed with the guidance of a crystallographer when necessary. The occupancies of the molecules were refined based on electron densities using the free variables. The crystallographic refinement process includes the handling of disordered molecules. All non-hydrogen atoms were refined with anisotropic displacement parameters. Hydrogen atoms were placed in idealized positions and refined as rigid atoms with the relative isotropic displacement parameters.

Theoretical calculations
All density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using Becke’s three-parameter hybrid exchange function and the Lee-Yang-Paar correlation function (B3LYP) with a default threshold of 6–31+G(d,p) basis set as implemented in Gaussian 16 Revision B.01. TD-DFT vertical excitation energy calculations were carried out for the anthracene dimers extracted from crystal structures using long-range corrected hybrid functional with damped dispersion correction (ωB97X-D). The electrostatic potential maps, highest-energy occupied, and lowest-energy unoccupied molecular orbitals were plotted using GaussView 6.0. The orientation of the transition μ was evaluated by TD-DFT calculations. Using dummy atoms to define the x, y, and z axes, the dipole vector was found to lie along the short axis of the anthracene framework.

## Abstract

The origin and control of material dynamics are fundamental to understanding functional systems from molecular assemblies to engineered devices. The ability to actively control and directly visualize rapid chemical and structural changes in a single crystal remains a major challenge in solid-state chemistry, limiting our understanding of dynamic functions in molecular materials. Here, we report an anthracene-based molecular crystal platform that enables dual physical control of solid-state [4+4] photocycloaddition through temperature and light. Chemically engineered 1,8-bis(pentafluorophenyl)anthracene single crystals construct photoactive face-to-face π-stacks, allowing the reaction to be induced by visible-light irradiation. Thus, exploring trans-scale crystal dynamics not only satisfies academic curiosity but also drives progress toward the development of materials with finely controlled kinetic response systems. Here, we report trans-scale crystal dynamics for the interdisciplinary control of kinetic responses by chemically and physically designing the anthracene molecular arrangement within a single crystal. By utilizing the physical quantity of temperature and irradiated light to control dynamic response time, we have successfully interpreted the dynamic process through the gradual changes in the crystal structure. Building on these results, we have discovered a method for frequency based on the efficiency of the interaction between the electric field of light and the anisotropic molecular orientation within the crystal lattice.

## Results

Chemical approaches for crystal dynamics
The importance of controlling crystal dynamics through photoactivation lies in the ability to construct reactive molecular assemblies that offer high reproducibility, along with a phase transition system that enables direct observation of dynamic processes. The [4+4] photocycloaddition of anthracene represents an ideal molecular system, wherein ON–OFF structural changes can be chemically and strategically induced by modifying the substituents. To achieve a photoinduced single-crystal-to-single-crystal phase transition in anthracene derivatives, precise control over bimolecular aggregation and crystal packing is essential. We targeted a face-to-face anthracene arrangement—favorable for photodimerization—by introducing substituents at the 1,8-positions along the short axis. The minimum face-to-face π-stacked structure required for the ON reaction has been identified based on data from the crystal structure database, previous literature, and our own study using molecular electrostatic potential maps. Electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups were selected to tune intermolecular interactions, thereby steering the packing toward either face-to-face or edge-to-face conformations. 1,8-Bis(perfluorophenyl)anthracene (1) was prepared by direct arylation (75% yield), while 1,8-bis(4-fluorophenyl)anthracene (2), 1,8-bisphenylanthracene (3), 1,8-bis(4-methylphenyl)anthracene (4), and 1,8-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)anthracene (5) were synthesized by Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling (58–98% yields). Vapor diffusion or solvent evaporation afforded single crystals (1_CCDC:2456683, 2_CCDC:2456863, 3a_CCDC:2456867, 3b_CCDC:2456866, 4_CCDC:2456864, and 5_CCDC:2456865). Depending on the choice of electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups, 1,8-diarylanthracene adopts either an ON (face-to-face) or OFF (edge-to-face) stacking structure in crystal.

1,8-Bis(pentafluorophenyl)anthracene (1) (Fig. 2a), which promotes selective face-to-face stacking through the introduction of electron-withdrawing groups and exhibits a characteristic optical absorption band, demonstrates ON behavior in crystal dynamics upon visible light irradiation. At 303 K, the centroid–centroid distances between the anthracene units in Unit 1 and Unit 2 are 3.818 and 4.667 Å, with corresponding overlap ratios of 41% and 33%, respectively. Notably, the centroid–centroid distance in Unit 1 is less than 4.2 Å, satisfying Schmidt’s criterion for [4+4] photocycloaddition. These results demonstrate that photodimerization occurs selectively at the Unit 1 site within a single crystal upon light irradiation. The resulting photodimer (1_PD) forms specifically at this position. Although the 1_PD crystals retain the original space group P2₁/c, Raman spectroscopy reveals changes in intra- and intermolecular vibrational modes, indicating modifications to both the chemical structure and crystal lattice. A Raman-active intramolecular vibrational mode at 329 cm⁻¹ was observed, arising from the C–C single bond formed through photodimerization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reverse transformation from crystalline 1_PD to crystalline 1 is feasible. This reversal was achieved by flash vacuum pyrolysis, in which specific molecular bonds are cleaved by a momentary high-temperature treatment. The results of this reverse reaction were also confirmed by NMR and single crystal structure analysis. These findings indicate that crystal dynamics can be reversibly controlled by the combined use of light and heat. These findings provide direct evidence for previously unobserved trans-scale crystal dynamics, governed by light-induced structural switching and kinetic control.

Thermal control of crystal dynamics
As crystal dynamics arise from the release of lattice strain accumulated during dimerization, thermal expansion or contraction of the unit cell induces the buildup of such strain. To investigate this, we performed variable-temperature single-crystal X-ray diffraction of crystal 1 from 103 to 303 K, evaluating atomic displacement parameters (U_eq) and crystallographic thermal expansion. With increasing temperature, two key changes were observed: (1) U_eq values of C9 and C10—atoms directly involved in anthracene photodimerization—increased, and (2) the reaction gap widened due to increased intermolecular distances (d_centroid-centroid, d_π-π, d_parallel) between Units 1 and 2. Expansion of the gap between π-stacks also induced anisotropic thermal expansion along the crystallographic c-axis and a reduction in the β angle. The temperature dependence of the photoreaction under white LED irradiation reveals that the crystal undergoes anisotropic deformation of the unit lattice as the temperature increases. It shows an “OFF: dormant state” between 103 and 203 K, during which no reaction occurs over 360 s, while a “ON: photoactive state” is observed between 253 and 353 K. Interestingly, the response time decreases with increasing temperature. Notably, under these conditions, crystal dynamics can be controlled in an ON–OFF manner by using temperature as a secondary physical parameter.

Optical control of crystal dynamics
The response time can also be modulated by photophysical parameters such as light intensity and wavelength. In contrast to white LED irradiation at room temperature (298 ± 5 K), UV light irradiation caused severe crystal collapse, including jumping, fragmentation, explosion, splintering, cracking, and splitting. Simultaneously, the emission color shifted from green to blue with increasing light exposure time. Single crystal X-ray structural analysis confirmed that the crystal obtained by UV irradiation (CCDC: 2483421) was structurally and chemically identical to the final product obtained by white LED irradiation, 1_PD. Similar behavior was observed under blue laser or sunlight exposure, though the response speed varied depending on the light source. Historically, the [4+4] photocycloaddition in crystals was proposed to require reactive sites to be within 4.2 Å of each other, and this was verified using UV light. Whereas crystal dynamics were previously accessible essentially under UV light, the discovery of systems responsive to visible light has enabled a more hierarchical and detailed understanding of photoinduced single-crystal-to-single-crystal phase transition-based dynamic processes. This UV-visible-driven dynamic crystal may exhibit varying phase transition ratios depending on the light wavelength. Powder X-ray diffraction measurements under UV irradiation at room temperature revealed that the diffraction intensity of the {020} reflection of crystalline 1 gradually disappeared with increasing irradiation time. This observation indicates a structural transition from crystalline 1 to crystalline 1_PD under UV irradiation. The {020} reflection from crystal 1 completely disappeared within approximately 210 s, demonstrating the quantitative transformation to crystal 1_PD. Under white LED irradiation, however, the phase transition (conversion) rate reached only about 50% within a comparable irradiation time. This difference arises from the higher absorption coefficient of UV light relative to visible light, confirming that the phase transition rate depends on the wavelength of the incident light. The absorption edge of one crystal, calculated from the fluorescence excitation spectrum, was found to be 470 nm, indicating a clear response to visible light.

Observation of intermediate states
While the mechanism of crystal dynamics was previously inferred by comparing crystal structures before and after the reaction, the stepwise photoreaction of the crystal, induced by white LED irradiation (a weak excitation light source) at room temperature, allows for direct observation of intermediate states, providing insights into the mechanism. The state corresponds to a mixed crystal 1·1_PD (x, y) with a nonstoichiometric composition, where crystals 1 and 1_PD coexist. The lattice parameter decreased linearly with increasing conversion ratio y. As unit 1 is progressively replaced by 1_PD, Vegard’s law predicts values of y as 0.87 and 0.92 at 480 and 540 s, respectively, based on the lattice constant a. The kinetics evaluated by the Johnson–Mehl–Avrami–Kolmogorov (JMAK) equation were determined to be k = 3.5 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ and n = 1.3. Since n > 1, it was shown that 1_PD formed in the crystal acts as an autocatalyst for unreacted Unit 1. Photoinduced crystal dynamics based on the process of releasing the lattice strain stored by the photoproduct to the outside reveal the correlation between the conversion ratio of the intermediate state and the lattice strain (Δa/a_0, Δb/b_0, Δc/c_0) and the change in the lattice constants (Δa, Δb, Δc), leading to their control. While Δb/b_0 and Δc/c_0 change very little with increasing y, Δa/a_0 decreases significantly with increasing y, indicating that lattice strain accumulates in the crystallographic a-axis direction as the photoreaction progresses. At this constant temperature, photoinduced lattice deformation reduces the β angle like the heating process. The identification of this correlation between the conversion ratio and lattice strain supports the mechanism by which thermally controlled ON/OFF crystal dynamics and response speed are driven by the promotion of lattice strain storage as the temperature increases.

Directional photodynamic control in crystal
The origin of this dynamic process suggests that the orientational light absorption efficiency of the higher-order structure controls the reaction probability. The crystal structure reveals that the transition dipole moment (μ), which correlates with the absorption coefficient (allowed transition), is oriented along the short axis of anthracene for both Unit 1 and Unit 2. Thus, μ is oriented along the crystallographic b-axis. Because the interaction between μ and the incident electric field depends on their relative orientation, the optical absorption of the crystal is inherently anisotropic. This orientation of μ induces anisotropic optical absorption, as the efficiency of the interaction between the electric field and μ varies with the relative alignment (parallel or perpendicular) between the polarization of the incident light and μ. Light irradiation along the [010] direction results in isotropic light absorption, as the polarized light propagating in this direction is perpendicular to μ. In contrast, light irradiation along the [001] direction leads to anisotropic light absorption, as the polarized light in this direction is parallel to μ. To further explore the anisotropic nature of the reaction, we investigated the effect of light polarization on the [001] and [010] crystal planes using a white LED. Along the [010] direction, no color was observed regardless of the polarization angle, indicating isotropic light absorption for this orientation. In contrast, the [001] direction exhibited coloration at polarization angles of 0° and 180°, whereas no color appeared between 50° and 130°. These results qualitatively demonstrate anisotropic light absorption along the [001] direction, and the observed polarization dependence is consistent with the theoretically predicted orientation of μ. The photoreactive frequency factor and response time exhibit different dynamic behaviors depending on the crystal plane direction of light irradiation, due to the anisotropic molecular orientation and alignment of the molecular crystals. The frequency and response time of white LED irradiation on each plane of a single crystal were 39% of the total in the [001] direction, while they were 90% of the total in the [010] direction. These results statistically show that the [010] direction has a higher probability of occurrence than the [001] direction. The response times for the [001] direction ranged from 30 to 176 s, with a mean of 94 ± 35 s (mean ± SD, n = 90). In contrast, the response times for the [010] direction ranged from 5 to 121 s, with a mean of 34 ± 18 s (mean ± SD, n = 39). The response time is statistically shorter in the [010] direction than in the [001] direction. Since the strength of μ correlates with the efficiency of light absorption, both its direction and strength are important parameters for controlling the photoreaction rate in the solid phase. Designing both the direction and strength of μ offers the potential for even greater precision.

In summary, we have demonstrated that a trans-scale strategy, which combines appropriate physical parameters (temperature, light intensity, wavelength, and direction) with a chemical approach and a multiscale understanding of behavior from the nano- to meso- to macro-scale, can enable the control of crystal dynamics. This strategy may be applied to understanding the origin of photoreaction processes in living organisms and to controlling systems made of solid materials. Controlling physical functions based on the atomic–molecular coordinate information of a crystal structure represents a significant challenge in developing material-motion-responsive systems. We have already succeeded in providing the necessary physical parameters, which could lead to the discovery of operational dynamic devices spanning nano- to meso- to macro-scale response systems.

---

## Methods

Materials
Solvents and reagents were purchased from Tokyo Chemical Industry Co., Sigma-Aldrich Co., LLC, Kanto Chemical Co., Inc., and FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical. 1 was prepared by direct arylation. Purified water was obtained using an ion exchange method (Pureline WL200, Yamato Scientific). The ion exchanger resin cartridge (CPC-P) had a capacity of 2 L and contained activated carbon. The water sample had a conductivity of 0.04 × 10⁻⁴ S/m.

Equipment
¹H and ¹³C NMR spectra were recorded on a JEOL JNM-ECZ400S spectrometer and Bruker Ascend-400 spectrometers. Ultraviolet-visible (UV–vis) absorption spectroscopy was performed using a JASCO V-650 spectrophotometer. Fluorescence excitation and photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy were conducted using a JASCO FP-8300 fluorescence spectrophotometer. Optical microscopy images and movies were acquired using a SHIMADZU Moticam 1080BMH equipped with a UV lamp (365 nm, 66 mW), a microscopic photoluminescence (µ-PL) spectroscopy system with a blue laser (405 nm, 5 µW), and a KEYENCE VHX-S8000 equipped with a white LED (4 mW). Light source spectra were measured using a Color Compass MFA. The power of the light sources was measured using a Field Mate laser power meter with a PM10 power sensor. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction measurements were performed using a Rigaku XtaLAB Synergy-S/Mo system (MoKα radiation, λ = 0.71073 Å) equipped with a HyPix-600HE photon counting detector and processed using the Olex2 software package. Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were carried out using a Rigaku SmartLab diffractometer with graphite-monochromatized CuKα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å). Raman spectroscopy was conducted using a HORIBA Jobin-Yvon LabRAM HR800 spectrometer, employing an Nd:YAG laser (λ = 532 nm) as the excitation source. An area of approximately 30 µm on the sample was irradiated through a D2 filter using a 50× objective lens. A microscope-compatible cooling/heating stage (Linkam model 10002L) was used under a nitrogen atmosphere over the temperature range of 103 K–353 K.

Single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis
The reduction and correction of the diffraction data were performed using the CrysAlisPro program. The structure was solved with the ShelXT structures solution program using Intrinsic Phasing. The structure was refined with the ShelXL refinement package using Least Squares minimization. Any alerts in the CIF should be carefully addressed with the guidance of a crystallographer when necessary. The occupancies of the molecules were refined based on electron densities using the free variables. The crystallographic refinement process includes the handling of disordered molecules. All non-hydrogen atoms were refined with anisotropic displacement parameters. Hydrogen atoms were placed in idealized positions and refined as rigid atoms with the relative isotropic displacement parameters.

Theoretical calculations
All density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using Becke’s three-parameter hybrid exchange function and the Lee-Yang-Paar correlation function (B3LYP) with a default threshold of 6–31+G(d,p) basis set as implemented in Gaussian 16 Revision B.01. TD-DFT vertical excitation energy calculations were carried out for the anthracene dimers extracted from crystal structures using long-range corrected hybrid functional with damped dispersion correction (ωB97X-D). The electrostatic potential maps, highest-energy occupied, and lowest-energy unoccupied molecular orbitals were plotted using GaussView 6.0. The orientation of the transition μ was evaluated by TD-DFT calculations. Using dummy atoms to define the x, y, and z axes, the dipole vector was found to lie along the short axis of the anthracene framework.

JMAK equation
Photochemical reaction in a single crystal was modeled using the JMAK equation.

y = 1 − e⁻(kt)n (1)

where y is the conversion ratio for the 1_PD, k is the reaction ratio constant, t is the irradiation time, and n is the Avrami exponent (reaction order).

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript presents a compelling interdisciplinary study on trans-scale crystal dynamics in anthracene derivatives, demonstrating innovative control of solid-state kinetics through chemical design and physical parameters (light direction, temperature). The work provides valuable mechanistic insights into photoinduced lattice strain and anisotropic responses. While scientifically sound and suitable for publication, minor revisions are required to enhance clarity, rigor, and presentation consistency.
1. In the manuscript, the crystal dynamics in photoreaction processes of crystal 1 was comprehensively studied. However, crystal 2-5 as control samples were rarely mentioned. The authors should add some discussion to explain the meanings of each crystal reported in the article.
2. The severe crystal collapse observed under UV light compared to visible light/LED is attributed to the light wavelength. However, UV light sources often have significantly higher photon energies and potentially higher intensities (power densities) than the visible light sources used (white LED, blue laser, sunlight). The manuscript does not report the incident light intensities/power densities for the different sources used in these comparative experiments. The authors should reconsider this issue.
3. In the temperature dependence of the photoreaction, the authors claimed that：“each temperature point represents the average response time of up to three crystals“. Such sample size is not enough for statistical experiment, which is recommended to be increased to 10 or more.
4. Spelling mistake: “Date ware” (Fig.4 caption) → “Data were”
5. please confirm the format of the references.
6. Some literature (Research 2024, 7, 0411; Adv. Sci. 2025, 12, e09088) should be added to reflect the research breadth of the work.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript presents an interesting study on anthracene-based crystals that show stimuli-responsive behavior through light-induced dimerization. Although this is a well-known photochemical reaction and have been previously used as a solid platform for exploring dynamic structural changes in the solid state, in this manuscript the authors introduce a dual control mechanism—using both heat and light—to modulate the crystal’s response, allowing the visualization of intermediate states, which is a notable achievement.
However, despite these strengths, the manuscript has several issues that make it unsuitable for publication in a high-impact journal in its current form:
Comments
1) The abstract lacks specificity and fails to clearly state the focus on anthracene derivatives or highlight the key findings—namely, dual control and intermediate state visualization. Instead, it relies on vague references to biological systems, which are not directly relevant and overgeneralize the study’s implications. It should be rewritten accordingly.
2) The rationale behind the selection and design of the anthracene derivatives is not explained. Although several anthracene derivatives are synthesized and characterized, in the manuscript their specific roles are unclear. A schematic framework is needed to clarify how these derivatives contribute to the study’s objectives.
3) As the author notes, identifying the relative orientation between light propagation and the molecular transition dipole moment as a control parameter in the photodynamic process is potentially significant. However, this concept is underdeveloped in the manuscript. To substantiate its importance, the authors should provide more robust theoretical/experimental evidence than simple statistics.
4) Several figures in the Supporting Information are either incorrectly referenced or not well integrated into the main text. This weakens the clarity and coherence of the experimental narrative. Proper cross-referencing and clearer integration are needed to improve consistency and readability throughout the manuscript. For example, in page 3 the authors mention: “Raman spectroscopy reveals changes in intra- and intermolecular vibrational modes (Supplementary Fig. 18), indicating modifications to both the chemical structure and crystal lattice (Supplementary Figs. 19–21 and Supplementary Table 8)”. On the one hand, Supplementary Fig. 18 presents only two Raman spectra without any accompanying discussion of the observed differences, which limits its usefulness in supporting the claims made in the main text. On the other hand, Supplementary Figs. 19–20 primarily focus on the solid-state retro reaction, including thermal analysis (DSC and TGA), the experimental setup, and NMR characterization of the final product—none of which directly support the discussion on changes in chemical structure or crystal lattice. This misalignment highlights the need for more accurate and purposeful cross-referencing of the supplementary materials. Considering the substantial volume of Supporting Information provided, and to improve overall readability and coherence, the manuscript should be carefully revised to ensure that each supplementary figure and table is clearly and correctly cited in context, and that the integration of this material meaningfully supports the corresponding sections of the main text.
5) The authors study the transformation under different light sources; however, these reactions appear to proceed more rapidly and, in some cases, lead to the rapid breakdown of the crystals. It remains unclear whether the final phases obtained under these alternative light sources are the same as those formed under white LED light. The authors should clarify whether the photoproducts are structurally and chemically identical across different irradiation conditions, and, if not, provide a discussion on the observed differences and their implications.
In summary: While the results are of scientific interest a more focused presentation and clearer methodological framing are needed to meet the standards of a high-impact journal.

### Reviewer 3

In the manuscript titled “Trans-scale crystal dynamics for controlling kinetic responses in organic molecular systems”, Hino et al. report temperature-dependent, photoinduced crystal dynamics in anthracene derivative crystals.
A key highlight of the study is the controlled modulation of crystal behavior through the relative orientation between the light propagation direction and the molecular transition dipole moment.
The work is intriguing and of have relevance to the field of dynamic molecular crystals. However, I recommend major revision before the manuscript can be considered for publication. The following points should be addressed to improve clarity, completeness, and presentation:
1. The abstract is too general and lacks a concise summary of the actual experimental work carried out. Instead of briefly stating the methodology or system studied, the abstract reads more like a conclusion. This diminishes clarity for readers attempting to understand the work from the outset.
2. The manuscript lacks a systematic description. For instance, it is not clearly stated how many anthracene derivatives were synthesized and studied, or the rationale behind their selection. The use of abbreviations should also be defined clearly at the beginning. From Figure 1 and the Supplementary Information (SI), it appears that five derivatives were investigated, but this should be clearly presented in the main text.
3. There is excessive referencing to the SI, which makes reading cumbersome. For example:
The sentence: “Depending on the choice of substituents, 1,8-diarylanthracene adopts either an ON (face-to-face) or OFF (edge-to-face) stacking structure (Supplementary Tables 1–6)” directs the reader across six different supplementary tables. A consolidated explanation in the main text summarizing this trend would help.
Similarly, the statement: “The minimum face-to-face π-stacked structure required for the ON reaction has been identified based on data from the crystal structure database, previous literature, and our own study using molecular electrostatic potential maps (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Figs. 1–13)” references 13 supplementary figures. Such heavy dependence on SI should be minimized by integrating key insights and summaries into the main text.
4. The sentence: “The discovery of crystal dynamics driven by visible light overcomes previous limitations related to light wavelength, enabling a more hierarchical and in-depth understanding of the dynamic process.” is unclear and should be elaborated. What limitations were previously imposed by light wavelength, and how does visible light resolve them?
5. The manuscript would benefit from a more detailed explanation of what exactly constitutes the ON and OFF states in terms of molecular stacking and crystal structure. These structural transitions are central to the work but are only briefly mentioned.
6. It is stated that UV light irradiation caused dramatic physical responses such as jumping, fragmentation, explosion, splintering, cracking, and splitting. But no detailed mechanism or conditions under which these movements occur is provided. Moreover, the photographic evidence (e.g., in the SI) is insufficient to clearly distinguish these effects.
7. The statement that “the crystal may exhibit varying phase transition ratios depending on the light wavelength” is not substantiated with any mechanistic explanation or data discussion. The authors should clarify the origin of this behavior.
8. Crucial details such as the intensity (power density) of the light sources used (UV, white LED, laser) are not provided. These are essential for reproducibility and understanding the kinetics.
9. Among three crystals irradiated, only one shows cracking. The authors should discuss why the other two did not respond similarly. Could crystal size or morphology be influencing the mechanical response? A brief analysis or hypothesis on size-dependence would add value.
10. The manuscript states that the transition dipole moment is oriented along the crystallographic b-axis. However, a more detailed explanation is needed on how μ is calculated or estimated from the crystal structure.
11. The manuscript focuses on the direction of the transition dipole moment but does not discuss how its magnitude might influence the photoinduced response. A brief discussion of whether higher μ would correlate with stronger or faster response would be useful, especially in the context of designing molecules for better dynamic behavior.

==== > We apologize for the insufficient description in our previous manuscript. The direction of the
transition dipole moment (μ) was estimated based on crystal structure and electronic structure analyses.

clarification demonstrates that our estimation method is based on a combination of TD-DFT calculations and
